name: Skylabs
description: Avionics and ground-station PCBs for flight logging and live LoRa telemetry.

paragraphs.heading: My work
paragraphs: I joined UNSW Skylabs in August 2025 and became Avionics & Payload Team Lead in May 2026. I represented UNSW at AIAA Design/Build/Fly 2026 in Wichita.
My work covers both ends of the link: the STM32 aircraft logger, the ESP32 LoRa ground station and the replay tools used after landing.

paragraphs.heading: Logging and flight replay
paragraphs: The aircraft binary log is the high-rate record, with a 40 Hz target. A smaller telemetry packet crosses the 915 MHz link at up to 10 Hz, where the ground station records it again and forwards a live stream over USB or its own Wi-Fi dashboard.

After the flight, the same data contract feeds a replay tool with the 3D route, attitude, artificial horizon, altitude, speed and GPS readouts kept on one timeline. Treating the boards, packet format and analysis software as one system has made faults much easier to trace.

images.alt: Skylabs aircraft telemetry circuit board

evidence.title: From aircraft sensors to a flight record
evidence.role: I developed the STM32 aircraft logger, ESP32 LoRa ground station and post-flight replay tools. I joined Skylabs in August 2025 and became Avionics & Payload Team Lead in May 2026.
evidence.problem: Sensors update at different rates, the radio carries a smaller live subset, and the team still needs a useful record after landing.
decisions: Keep the aircraft binary log separate from the live link. Record the received packets again on the ground, then use one data contract for synchronized replay.
evidence.validation: The published F110211 flight contains 13,772 rows over 679.33 seconds. Its report records a 50.0 ms log interval, 13,402 log overruns and zero SD write errors.
evidence.limit: 40 Hz is the aircraft logger’s target. This flight does not demonstrate sustained 40 Hz logging; zero SD write errors does not mean every timing deadline was met.

name: Kiku
description: A pocket audio player for SD music, FM radio and Bluetooth receiving.
spec: Real firmware simulator · Nine-part CAD explorer

images.alt: Kiku P2 source-CAD player with a cream shell, green dial, orange key and captured firmware screen
Source display assembly guide identifying the protective lens, LCD, cradle and flex connection

evidence.title: Audio architecture
evidence.role: Circuit design, embedded firmware and enclosure development. Personal project, 2026.
evidence.maturity: Working development hardware · P2 enclosure awaiting physical fit check
evidence.problem: Bring local files, FM radio and Bluetooth receiving into one tactile, handheld player.
decisions: The STM32H523 brings three listening sources into a common 48 kHz PCM output domain for wired headphones and the built-in speaker. The BM83 receives Bluetooth audio from a phone; there is no transmit path to wireless headphones.
Audio DMA has a 2 ms service window. An 8,192-frame stereo FIFO provides roughly 171 ms of buffering, with local playback filled ahead of display work. The screen only sends the region that changed.

A push encoder and two keys control the interface, with ten selectable looks. The browser simulator runs the actual C screen renderer compiled to WebAssembly; its hardware events, library and radio data are simulated.
The nine-part P2 enclosure develops the printed P1 design with a larger battery bay, stronger port opening, removable display cradle and folding stand.
evidence.validation: The 12 October 2026 firmware record includes a clean build, host tests, 130 renderer captures and flash readback verification. The renderer captures passed bounds and full-frame versus dirty-region equivalence checks.
evidence.limit: These checks establish the tested firmware image and behaviour, not extended listening reliability or physical fit. Longer Bluetooth playback, SD insertion, output switching, power measurements and a P2 assembly test remain on the bench. The browser does not receive FM or pair over Bluetooth, and its demo music is separate from the STM32 audio pipeline.
evidence.challenges: The display sits in a removable cradle behind a 1 mm clear lens. Its flex follows a U-fold studied at roughly 4.3 mm bend radius. Supplier contact dimensions and connector insertion geometry still need a real mating check.

hero.alt: Kiku P2 source-CAD player, with cream shell, green dial and firmware display

name: TramTrace
description: A live LED map of Sydney and Parramatta light rail, built around an ESP32.

paragraphs.heading: Metroboard's sibling
paragraphs: Metroboard covered Sydney's heavy-rail network, so the obvious follow-up was the tram network. TramTrace squeezes the CBD and Parramatta lines onto a smaller board without turning the route into an unreadable knot.
The board joins Wi-Fi and gets vehicle positions from a small service I wrote. The LEDs then turn those positions into something I can read at a glance from across the room.

paragraphs.heading: On the board
paragraphs: An ESP32-WROOM-32E handles the network connection and display logic. A CH340C gives me a straightforward USB programming path, while level shifting keeps the ESP32 and LED data happy together.

The hard part was physical rather than computational: the station names, route geometry and components all had to share the same compact board. The silkscreen ended up doing real work as part map, part assembly drawing.

name: Dual USB-C Framework Card
description: One laptop expansion bay turned into two USB 2.0 Type-C ports.

paragraphs.heading: Two ports in one bay
paragraphs: A normal expansion card spends the whole bay on one connector. I wanted two. USB 2.0 was enough for the small peripherals I actually plug in, and keeping the scope there made the routing and power design realistic in the Framework card outline.
The finished board fits the standard clear shell, so it looks and behaves like the other modules instead of hanging off the laptop as an adapter.

paragraphs.heading: The circuit
paragraphs: A CH334F handles the two-port hub. The TPS2065 switches and limits downstream power, and USBLC6-2SC6 parts sit close to the connectors for ESD protection. I also had to fit the crystal, configuration resistors and three Type-C connectors into a board that is mostly connector.
The layout is dense but still readable. The clear case makes that worthwhile: you can see the hub and power path when the card is installed.

name: Framework ESP32 Card
description: An ESP32-S3 squeezed into a black Framework expansion-card PCB.

paragraphs.heading: A laptop-bay dev board
paragraphs: I liked the Framework expansion-card system, but I wanted a module that could do more than expose another laptop port. This one puts an ESP32-S3-MINI-1 in the bay and leaves the radio visible through a clear shell.
The 0.6 mm board thickness is part of the electrical design as much as the mechanical one: it lets the card mate with the laptop's USB-C connector without a separate plug or interposer.
The latest revision swaps the original green board for black solder mask and white silkscreen. It is now assembled in the clear enclosure, with the antenna end of the ESP32 left unobstructed.

paragraphs.heading: Programming and power
paragraphs: A CH340K provides the USB serial connection. The BC817 transistor pair handles automatic boot and reset, so uploading firmware feels like using a normal development board rather than a bare module.
An AMS1117-3.3 supplies the ESP32. None of those parts are exotic; fitting them, the USB routing and the module keep-out into the expansion-card outline was the real exercise.

name: Framework Logic Analyser
description: An STM32 logic analyser with logic, serial-bus and passive CAN capture in a Framework expansion card.

paragraphs.heading: Capture interfaces
paragraphs: The card brings logic and serial-bus capture into a Framework expansion bay. Its STM32G474 supports four-channel logic and SPI capture, two-channel UART and I²C capture, and passive monitoring of CAN, RS-485 and RS-422.
The firmware documents a maximum capture rate of 10 MS/s and a buffer of 32,768 samples. Those limits describe the acquisition modes; they do not imply that every protocol runs at the maximum rate.

paragraphs.heading: Signal routing
paragraphs: Two MAX14778 multiplexers route the inputs. A TCAN3413 handles the CAN interface, while a THVD4411 provides the multiprotocol transceiver. A seven-pin connector brings the signals and power to the edge of the card.
The four-layer PCB measures 26 × 30 mm.

images.alt: Framework Logic Analyser

evidence.title: Capture hardware with explicit safe states
evidence.role: An STM32G474 card design with board-specific capture firmware and Python host tooling.
evidence.media_label: CAD render · published firmware and host tests
evidence.problem: Bring logic and serial-bus capture into a 26 × 30 mm expansion card while keeping passive monitoring from driving the bus under observation.
decisions: Timer-triggered DMA samples the GPIO inputs. Native USB CDC carries commands and captured bytes to a Python tool that exports VCD or CSV.
The firmware boots with the muxes disconnected, CAN in standby and the multiprotocol transceiver shut down. Route changes disable the drivers before reconnecting inputs.
Raw GPIO routes are limited to 3.3 V logic. RS-232 is excluded from passive capture because that transceiver mode also enables its transmitter.
evidence.validation: Published host-side tests exercise binary framing, VCD/CSV export and command validation using simulated serial data. The hardware document maps firmware pins and safe states to the routed PCB.
evidence.outcome: The prototype firmware implements immediate capture with configured limits of 10 MS/s and 32,768 samples, plus passive Classical CAN monitoring. Hardware trigger and pre-trigger capture remain unimplemented.

name: RGB Drink Coaster
description: A 24-pixel STM32 coaster that reacts to cup shadow and local temperature change.

paragraphs.heading: Detect the drink
paragraphs: The VEML7700 sits near the centre of the board and turns the cup's shadow into a placement signal. At startup the firmware learns the uncovered light level for two seconds. A drop to 65% or less of that reference for 500 ms marks the coaster occupied; light returning to at least 85% for 500 ms marks it empty again.

That makes the same sensor useful for both presence and brightness without adding a switch or load cell. The trade-off is optical: room-light changes, clear cups and RGB reflections through the lid can all affect the reading, so the firmware uses hysteresis and minimum-light thresholds rather than treating every dip as a cup.

paragraphs.heading: Measure the change
paragraphs: An SHT4x tracks local temperature under the centre of the coaster. The sensor is separated from the cup by the enclosure: the clear lid is 3 mm thick and the CAD leaves about 2.7 mm between the package and the lid. The firmware therefore displays change at the PCB sensor instead of pretending it knows the drink's actual temperature.

While the coaster is empty, its temperature reference follows the room slowly. When a cup is placed, that reference freezes and small local changes shift the colour from cool tones through neutral to warm tones. Temperature and light are sampled four times per second while the LED frame updates at 40 fps.

paragraphs.heading: Firmware with two moods
paragraphs: The default build keeps a calm six-second travelling highlight around the ring. A separate Drink Companion build adds a rainbow welcome, cool glints, warm embers, an aurora and a goodbye sparkle while keeping the same sensor and fault logic.

Both current images have been flash-verified on the assembled board. The fun build at source commit 9da0988 was also observed running at about 3.26 V with temperature, humidity, ambient-light, WHITE-channel and LED-frame counters advancing without recorded sensor or LED-transfer errors. Cup behaviour through the clear resin and the final thermal response still need physical tuning.

name: RF Test Board
description: Feedlines and filter footprints made to be compared on a VNA.

paragraphs.heading: Test setup
paragraphs: The useful RF advice is usually short: control the impedance, keep the return path intact, and place the matching network close. What I wanted to know was how much each detail changed the result on the inexpensive two-layer process I was actually using.
I ordered this board without impedance control and measured it with a VNA. That gave me a physical reference for the manufacturer's stack-up instead of another calculator result.

paragraphs.heading: What I compared
paragraphs: The board carries straight coplanar traces, tuning-capacitor sections and split-pi filter footprints, with both u.FL and SMA transitions. It also repeats the feedline with and without solder mask.

The target was 50 Ω on 1.6 mm FR-4 with 1 oz outer copper and a 0.2 mm gap to the surrounding copper. The nominal trace widths printed on the back are 0.8877 mm with mask and 1.0244 mm without it. Keeping those numbers on the board means the sample stays useful after the design files have disappeared into an archive.

SMA end of the RF test PCB with filter and tuning footprints
Back of the RF test board with revision title

evidence.title: A physical check on the RF layout
evidence.role: A two-layer RF comparison board, ordered without impedance control and measured with a vector network analyser.
evidence.media_label: Manufactured test-board photography · interactive CAD assembly
evidence.problem: Check calculated feedline geometry against the inexpensive 1.6 mm FR-4 fabrication process used for the preceding LoRa receiver.
decisions: Place masked and unmasked coplanar traces, u.FL and SMA transitions, tuning sections and split-pi footprints on the same board.
Print the stack-up and nominal trace widths on the reverse: 1 oz copper, a 0.2 mm ground gap, and widths of 0.8877 mm with mask and 1.0244 mm without it. The design target is 50 Ω.
evidence.challenges: The earlier LoRa receiver's Rev A feedline missed the intended 50 Ω impedance. Investigating it with a VNA led to this dedicated comparison board.
evidence.validation: VNA evaluation is documented in the project record. Photographs identify the comparison structures and the printed stack-up and geometry.
evidence.outcome: A reusable physical reference for comparing feedlines, connector transitions and filter footprints on the chosen fabrication process.

name: LoRa Receiver + GNSS
description: An ESP32 receiver board with a u-blox NEO-M9N and 915 MHz LoRa.

paragraphs.heading: Radio and position
paragraphs: I designed this board as one half of a small telemetry link. An ESP32-WROOM-32E runs the application, a 915 MHz LoRa module handles the long-range connection, and a u-blox NEO-M9N supplies position data.
Putting the radio and GNSS on one board kept the wiring simple in use. It also made the RF layout impossible to ignore, which turned out to be the more valuable part of the project.

paragraphs.heading: The first RF lesson
paragraphs: The Rev A feedline was not as close to 50 Ω as I wanted. I checked it with a VNA, took the mismatch seriously, and used what I found when I laid out the dedicated RF test board.
Even with that first-pass layout, the pair reached at least one kilometre in testing. That result was useful, but the measurement was better: it gave the next board a specific problem to fix.

name: Metroboard
description: A 300 × 305.7 mm Sydney rail map driven by live data and 291 LEDs.

paragraphs.heading: Sydney rail display
paragraphs: I wanted Sydney's rail network to live on the wall, not in another browser tab. Metroboard is a 300 × 305.7 mm PCB with 291 LEDs, laid out as a physical map of the network.

The board joins Wi-Fi and gets TfNSW GTFS real-time data through a service I wrote. Each update turns vehicle positions into light, so the useful part of the display is visible before I have even picked up my phone.

paragraphs.heading: The PCB is the interface
paragraphs: There is no separate screen or printed overlay. The copper, solder mask, silkscreen and LEDs have to work together as both electronics and map graphics.

That constraint is what later led to TramTrace. The tram network needed a different scale and much tighter route geometry, but the idea stayed the same: make live transport data legible as a piece of hardware.

name: LoRa Talkie
description: A one-button Morse message composer and handheld 915 MHz LoRa radio.

paragraphs.heading: One button, full messages
paragraphs: LoRa Talkie normally sits in receive mode and prints incoming messages straight to its OLED. A double-click opens the composer, where the same program button becomes a Morse key. I added dedicated patterns for spaces and deleting the last character so a complete message can be written without a keyboard.
A two-second hold sends the message and returns to the chat screen. The device remembers the last four outgoing messages; they can be selected with one to four clicks, edited and sent again.

paragraphs.heading: Radio and field controls
paragraphs: The current radio profile uses 915 MHz LoRa with a 250 kHz bandwidth, spreading factor 12 and up to 22 dBm transmit power. After each transmission the firmware puts the radio straight back into continuous receive mode.

The status page shows battery voltage, the configured frequency and spreading factor, transmit power and board temperature. There is also a repeating beacon mode for link checks, battery and temperature safety cut-offs, and deep sleep for carrying the unit without running it flat.
The OLED interface is deliberately small but not purely functional: it has startup and shutdown animations, plus coin, dice and slot-machine diversions that use the same single-button control scheme.

name: Dash
description: An ESP32 focus companion with animated eyes, gestures and app-free session control.

paragraphs.heading: From the car to the desk
paragraphs: Dash started as the vehicle-mounted safe-driving prototype shown in the photos below. I kept the useful hardware ideas—the ESP32, IMU, touch input, OLED, speaker and battery supply—but rebuilt the firmware around a different job: helping me stay focused at a desk.

The current version is a cube-shaped study companion. Its screen is a pair of animated eyes, so a tap, shake, change of orientation or completed session gets a reaction without turning the device into another notification-heavy display.

paragraphs.heading: The board underneath
paragraphs: The Driving Companion PCB measures 45.2 × 45.2 mm, with two copper layers on a 1.6 mm board. An ESP32-WROOM-32E connects to an MPU-6050 motion sensor, a four-pin display header and a MAX98357A audio amplifier for the speaker.

USB-C and a CH340C provide the wired programming interface. The battery supply combines TP4056 charging, DW01A / 8205A protection and a TPS62A01 regulator. Three mounting holes define the board's attachment points.

paragraphs.heading: Firmware
paragraphs: A single state machine coordinates the character, focus timer, games and low-power states. The MPU-6050 is sampled at 100 Hz for software tap and orientation detection, while separate tasks look after the OLED, audio, touch input and session timing.

Dash creates its own Wi-Fi access point and serves a captive portal from LittleFS, so a phone can start a study session, see recent stats and change settings without an app or account. Completed sessions are kept in a rolling on-device log, and in-progress sessions can survive a reset through RTC memory.

I also built reaction-time and gesture games, OTA update support and an ESP-NOW layer for experimenting with group sessions between nearby units. Power management drops the ESP32 from 240 to 80 MHz as Dash gets drowsy, then uses deep sleep when it has been left alone.

name: Aircraft telemetry
description: STM32 sensor acquisition, onboard logging and the aircraft side of a live LoRa link.

paragraphs.heading: Sensors and logging
paragraphs: I developed this PCB around an STM32G474RET6. It brings together a u-blox GNSS receiver, BNO08x IMU, BME280 barometer, digital and analogue airspeed inputs, an HX711 strain interface, RTC, microSD storage and an SX1262 radio.
Each sensor has its own useful rate, failure mode and definition of “fresh”. The firmware stores presence and validity beside each measurement; missing values are NaN, not zero.

paragraphs.heading: Firmware and logging
paragraphs: The IMU supplies acceleration and gyro reports at 100 Hz, attitude at 50 Hz and magnetometer data at 25 Hz. GNSS runs at 10 Hz. The aircraft logger samples at a 40 Hz target, batches eight binary records into each SD transaction and syncs once a second, which avoids making every sample wait for a card write.

A compact SX1262 packet carries the live subset to the ground station. The default profile sends at 22 dBm every 100 ms using 500 kHz bandwidth and spreading factor 5. Ground commands can start or stop the aircraft log, add an event marker and change the link profile without a USB cable in the aircraft.

paragraphs.heading: After landing
paragraphs: The binary record keeps GNSS, environment, attitude, airspeed, strain and estimator output together. My replay tool reads that file into a synchronized 3D path, aircraft attitude, artificial horizon and engineering plots, while leaving the recorded values untouched.

evidence.title: Separate the logging target from the flight result
evidence.role: STM32 aircraft PCB, sensor acquisition, binary logging and the aircraft side of the SX1262 telemetry link.
evidence.media_label: Assembled hardware photography · recorded flight evidence
evidence.problem: Keep a useful onboard record while sensors update at different rates and the radio carries only a smaller live subset.
decisions: Store sensor presence and validity beside the readings, with missing measurements represented as NaN.
After the reference flight, buffer eight records per SD write and run sensor capture and logging before radio service. The logging target remains 40 Hz.
Gate EKF outputs using uncertainty and plausibility checks. The replay uses valid GNSS horizontal position and barometric height for the reference flight.
evidence.challenges: The F110211 flight averaged 20.27 Hz against the 40 Hz target and recorded 13,402 logging overruns. Its navigation EKF diverged, so the EKF path is excluded from the flight analysis.
evidence.validation: The published diagnostic covers 679.331 seconds and 13,772 usable aircraft records, with a 50 ms median log interval and zero SD write errors. These storage and timing results are reported separately.
evidence.outcome: A later 150-second bench hold produced 146/146 fresh samples with continuous BNO and BME validity. The revised SD rate and EKF recovery still require confirmation in a fresh aircraft binary log.

name: Ground station
description: An ESP32 receiver, independent SD record and field interface for Skylabs.

paragraphs.heading: Ground station receiver
paragraphs: I developed the ground station around an ESP32-WROOM-32E, SX1262 radio, microSD socket and a Qwiic connector for the OLED. Two buttons and two activity LEDs keep the common field actions available even when nobody has a laptop open.

Every valid aircraft packet can be stored locally, so the team gets an independent copy of the live data even if the aircraft is damaged or its card is hard to reach. The board can write readable CSV or an indexed, CRC-protected binary format that can recover past a damaged record.

paragraphs.heading: Field workflow
paragraphs: The OLED cycles between an artificial horizon, link figures and sensor status. It shows RSSI, GPS and SD state, heading, satellite count and IMU accuracy instead of reducing the whole system to a single “connected” light.

The ESP32 also creates a Wi-Fi access point with a captive dashboard and pre-flight checklist. From a phone, the crew can inspect fresh telemetry, name a flight, choose the log format, add a marker or change the radio profile. Start and stop commands are repeated over LoRa so the aircraft and ground logs begin together.

paragraphs.heading: Aircraft, receiver and laptop logs
paragraphs: The receiver streams a rate-limited 230400-baud feed over USB without slowing the SD logger. A PC dashboard can record that stream as another CSV backup, while the onboard dashboard remains available when the laptop is not.
Giving the aircraft, receiver and laptop separate records costs some storage, but it has made flight-day problems much less mysterious.

evidence.title: A second record at the field
evidence.role: An ESP32-WROOM-32E ground-station PCB bringing together the SX1262 receiver, microSD storage, OLED connection and field controls.
evidence.problem: The crew needs telemetry and logging controls without depending on a laptop, plus a separate record if the aircraft log becomes inaccessible.
decisions: Store valid received packets locally as CSV or indexed, CRC-protected binary. Expose link and sensor status on the OLED, and provide a phone-ready Wi-Fi dashboard and pre-flight checklist.
evidence.validation: The published build photographs show the receiver, antenna connection and microSD hardware. The documented workflow adds a rate-limited USB stream for another record on a laptop.
evidence.limit: A ground log contains the received live subset, not the full aircraft log. No packet-loss benchmark or damaged-record recovery test result is published here.
